title: Copyright-Bench: Agentic Evaluation of Copyright Law Compliance
claim: Prompt framing strongly shifts violation rates: awareness cues sharply reduce them and dismissive cues raise them across agents and humans.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bar chart, 4 groups by 3 conditions, value labels
description: A single grouped bar chart with copyright violation rate (0–80%) on the y-axis. The x-axis has four groups: Human baseline, Claude 4.5 Opus, GPT-5.2 and Llama-4 Scout. Each group has three bars for prompt framing: Neutral (light blue), IP-aware (cream with diagonal hatching) and IP-dismissive (dark navy). A legend sits at the top right. Numeric labels sit above every bar. The IP-aware bars are consistently the lowest (2, 11, 13 and 25). The IP-dismissive bars are the tallest for the human baseline (48) and Llama-4 Scout (66). For Claude (21) and GPT (26), the IP-dismissive bars fall below Neutral (38 and 40). The eye goes first to the tall navy Llama bar at the far right, then to the hatched bars, which show the drop under awareness cues. Faint horizontal gridlines and a minimal frame keep the plot clean.
caption: Prompt framing strongly shapes agentic copyright compliance. Copyright violation rates under Neutral, IP-aware, and IP-dismissive prompts, averaged across the three task families in the standard environment.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform commercial tasks that involve retrieving external content such as images and, where appropriate, reproducing that content. LLM agents should comply with the law, including the laws of copyright. Yet today we lack adequate tools to assess whether they do so. To that end, we introduce Copyright-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate copyright law compliance of LLM agents. Copyright-Bench is comprised of realistic commercial tasks---website development, merchandise design, and corporate content production---that involve agents selecting between freely licensed content (the use of which is legal) and copyrighted content (the use of which is illegal at least in this setting). Notably, the evaluation introduces prompt variations that simulate different levels of user intent and time pressure. Comparing state-of-the-art agents against a human baseline, we find that: (1) LLM agents take actions that violate copyright law despite the availability of lawful alternatives; and (2) violation rates increase in response to user intent and under simulated time pressure.
